headline: Ran the Wilmington Elbow on a hunch — three yellowfin, one bigeye bite that got away
subhead: A warm Gulf Stream filament pushed further north than it should this late in July, and it's stacking bait right where we wanted it.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning I had a choice to make at the fuel dock: run straight out to the 28-fathom hump and chunk, or burn the extra diesel to the Elbow and troll the edge where I'd marked a hard break the week before. Chunking's cheaper and it's a sure bait draw, but with the boat full and a long ride ahead, I wanted moving baits in the water the second we hit color. We ran the troll. That decision paid for the fuel and then some.

The break was sitting right where I left it, holding around 38°34'N, 74°08'W on the northeast corner, with the temp gauge jumping from the mid-70s into the upper 70s in about a quarter mile — that's the kind of shelf water tuna use as a highway marker. This is the warm filament that's been the talk of every canyon from here down through Washington — it's pushed further north than you'd expect for the tail end of July, and it's dragging Gulf Stream water right up onto the edge instead of staying pinned south like it usually does this time of year. We flagged this exact pattern holding steady last week, and here it is, still doing its thing three days later.

We pulled a standard war spectrum — ballyhoo skirted in blue/white and green machine off the riggers, naked ballyhoo down the shotgun, spreader bar down the center — through the 100-fathom curve and out to about 250 fathoms where the bottom really falls off the shelf. Marked bait balls stacked up tight on the meter right on the thermocline around 90 feet, and it didn't take long. First yellowfin came on the long rigger around 9:15, a chunky 45-pounder that ate the naked ballyhoo clean. Two more came through mid-morning working the same stretch, both in the 35-50 pound class. Not a stacked bite by any stretch — we worked that edge for six hours and those three fish were it for hookups, though we had two more knockdowns we never connected on, one of which pulled drag hard enough and deep enough that I'd put money on bigeye. That's canyon fishing in late July: you get shots, you don't always close them.

Mahi were scattered but present wherever we found floating structure — a mat of sargassum about a mile off the break gave up two schoolies in the 8-10 pound range on small green machine spreader bars we dropped back after the tuna bite slowed. If you're running the edge and see any weed line or debris, even a five-gallon bucket or a pallet, it's worth the five-minute detour. Mahi are opportunistic right now, riding whatever shade they can find, and they don't need much of an excuse to show up in your spread.

White marlin gave us one legitimate look — a fish came up on the long teaser late morning, wouldn't commit to the pitch bait, and disappeared. That's been the pattern boats are reporting up and down this stretch: shots are there, conversions are spotty. If you're serious about marlin right now, I'd rig a dedicated pitch rod with a select ballyhoo and keep someone on it full-time rather than trying to run a mixed spread and react. The fish are eating slow and cautious in this warm, clean water — they're not crashing baits, they're inspecting them.

Wahoo have been quiet on our end this week, though we heard of one boat working the Baltimore Canyon side picking off a couple on high-speed lures worked deep along the drop. If wahoo are on your target list, I'd rig a couple of deep divers behind planers on the outside lines and let them ride below the main spread rather than dedicating the whole troll to them — they're a bonus fish right now, not a primary target.

The moon's coming off full and tides are easing toward neap over the next several days, which usually softens current on the edge a touch — that's not a bad thing for trolling since a moderate current keeps bait from getting blown off the break entirely. Wind's been light out of the southwest, seas comfortable, and that stable high-pressure pattern is exactly what's kept this warm filament pinned in place instead of sliding back south like it typically would this late in the month.

Looking at the next few days, I'd expect the status quo to hold through Saturday — steady yellowfin on the temp breaks, mahi wherever there's floating cover, and marlin shots for anyone willing to dedicate a rod to it. The bigger question is early next week, when the typical early-August frontal disturbance could roll through and stir things up for a day or two before the pattern re-establishes. If that happens, I wouldn't panic — these warm-water filaments have been resilient all month, and the bait's not going anywhere fast. My plan is to keep working the Elbow and adjust east or west a few miles based on where the sharpest color change sits that morning. If you're headed out, mark your break the day before if you can, because it's shifted a mile or two most days this week, and finding it early saves you fuel and gets baits in front of fish before the bite windows tighten up midday.
